---
title: "Quiz: back-projection and the Fourier slice theorem"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** What does back-projection do with one measured line integral?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
We do not know where on the ray the attenuation was.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It adds the value to every pixel on that ray (with the same weights the projector used to sum them). Not knowing where along the ray the material was, it spreads it evenly. Doing this for all rays of all angles and adding gives the back-projection.
:::

---

**Q2.** A single bright point is back-projected from 4 angles, then from 180. Describe both results.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Each angle contributes one stripe through the point.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
4 angles: a star of four stripes crossing at the point. 180 angles: a bright peak at the point surrounded by a halo that fades like $1/r$: the stripes overlap densely near the point and spread out with distance.
:::

---

**Q3.** Is back-projection the inverse of projection? What is it instead?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Write projection as $A\mathbf x$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. Projection is a matrix $A$; back-projection is its **transpose** $A^\top$. $A^\top A$ is not the identity but a blur (a $1/r$ kernel), so back-projecting a sinogram gives a blurred, unnormalised image.
:::

---

**Q4.** Why does the plain back-projection of a large uniform disc look brighter in the middle than at its rim, and glow outside it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Every point of the disc gets a halo.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Each point of the disc is blurred by the $1/r$ halo. A pixel in the middle receives halo contributions from disc points all around it; a pixel at the rim has disc on one side only; a pixel outside still receives the tails. So the middle is raised, the edge is soft and the surroundings glow.
:::

---

**Q5.** State the Fourier slice theorem in one sentence, without formulas.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The 1D spectrum of the projection taken at angle $\theta$ is the same as the 2D spectrum of the image along the straight line through its centre in the direction $\theta$.
:::

---

**Q6.** An image contains only horizontal stripes (the grey value changes along $y$). Which projection angle shows the stripes, and which shows a constant? Where are the stripes in the 2D spectrum?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
At $0°$ the rays are vertical.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
At $90°$ the rays are horizontal and run along each stripe: the projection (row sums) shows the stripes. At $0°$ every column crosses all stripes and averages them: constant. In the 2D spectrum the stripes are two dots on the vertical axis, which is the $90°$ slice.
:::

---

**Q7.** The theorem says projections fill the spectrum line by line. Why is "FFT each projection, place it on its line, inverse 2D FFT" not the standard method?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where are the samples, and where does the inverse FFT need them?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The samples lie on spokes, dense near the centre and sparse far out; the inverse FFT needs them on a Cartesian grid. Interpolating from spokes to grid introduces errors, and an error at one frequency is a wave over the whole image: the errors spread everywhere instead of staying local.
:::

---

**Q8.** How do the spokes of the Fourier slice theorem explain the halo of plain back-projection?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Every projection contributes a whole spoke through the centre, so the low frequencies near the centre are covered by every angle while the high frequencies far out are covered thinly. Back-projection adds all spokes with equal weight, so slow waves are over-represented, by a factor proportional to $1/|\omega|$. In the image that is the $1/r$ halo.
:::

---

**Q9.** *(math)* Prove the slice theorem for $\theta = 0$: $\int p_0(x)\,e^{-2\pi iux}\,dx = F(u, 0)$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$p_0(x) = \int f(x, y)\,dy$, so $\int p_0(x)e^{-2\pi iux}dx = \iint f(x, y)e^{-2\pi i(ux + 0\cdot y)}\,dx\,dy = F(u, 0)$. The factor $e^{-2\pi i\cdot 0\cdot y} = 1$ lets the integral over $y$ be done first.
:::
